Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\right)\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ \frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}27(t-1)+(3t+1) \\ 27(t-1)+3(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}30t-26 \\ 36t-24\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$

$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-{a}_{2}+2){t}^{2}+(-{b}_{2}+1)t+(-{c}_{2}+3) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}+2)t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
